subject: math
cluster: Use random sampling to draw inferences about a population
intro: A population is the whole group you want to learn about; a sample is the subset you actually examine. A conclusion about the population is trustworthy only when the sample is representative, and random sampling, where every member has an equal chance of being chosen, is what tends to produce representative samples. These problems progress from naming populations and samples to spotting bias and judging whether an inference is justified.

items.prompt: A principal wants to know the favorite school lunch of all $850$ students at a school. She surveys $50$ of those students. Identify the population and the sample.
items.answer: Population: all $850$ students at the school. Sample: the $50$ students who were surveyed.

steps: The population is the entire group you want to learn about. Here that is all $850$ students at the school.
The sample is the subset that is actually examined. Here that is the $50$ students who were surveyed.
So the population is the $850$ students and the sample is the $50$ surveyed students.

items.prompt: A factory makes $10{,}000$ light bulbs in a day. An inspector tests $200$ of them to estimate how many are defective. What is the population and what is the sample?
items.answer: Population: all $10{,}000$ light bulbs made that day. Sample: the $200$ bulbs the inspector tested.

steps: The population is the whole group of interest: all $10{,}000$ light bulbs made that day.
The sample is the part actually examined: the $200$ bulbs the inspector tested.
The inspector studies the sample of $200$ to draw a conclusion about the population of $10{,}000$.

items.prompt: To choose a sample, a teacher writes every student's name on an identical slip of paper, mixes the slips in a bag, and draws $10$ names without looking. Is this a random sample? Answer yes or no and give a one-sentence reason.
items.answer: Yes. It is random because mixing identical slips and drawing without looking gives every student an equal chance of being selected.

steps: A sample is random when every member of the population has an equal chance of being chosen.
Identical slips, thorough mixing, and drawing without looking mean no student is more or less likely to be picked.
Therefore this is a random sample.

items.prompt: A reporter stands at one exit of a stadium and interviews the first $20$ people who happen to walk past about the game. Is this a random sample or a convenience sample?

steps: A convenience sample is made of whoever is easiest to reach, not chosen by chance.
Interviewing the first $20$ people who walk past one exit picks people simply because they are nearby and available.
Since not every fan had an equal chance of being chosen, this is a convenience sample, not a random sample.

items.prompt: Fill in the blank with the correct word: A sample whose characteristics closely mirror those of the whole population is called a ______ sample.

steps: A sample that mirrors the make-up of the population is called a representative sample.
Random sampling is valued because it tends to produce representative samples.
The blank is filled with the word representative.

items.prompt: A radio station asks listeners to call in and vote on whether a new highway should be built. Name the type of sampling method this is, and state one reason it may be biased.
items.answer: Voluntary response sample. It may be biased because only people who feel strongly enough to call in respond, so their opinions may not match the whole community.

steps: When people choose for themselves whether to participate, the method is a voluntary response sample.
The cause of the bias is self-selection: those with strong feelings are far more likely to call in.
Because the respondents select themselves, the sample is unlikely to mirror the full community, so it is biased.

items.prompt: A city wants to know how all residents commute to work. A researcher surveys only people waiting at a downtown bus stop. Identify the source of bias and state its cause.
items.answer: The sample is biased because it only includes bus riders. Location bias: surveying at a bus stop oversamples people who commute by bus and misses people who drive, bike, or walk.

steps: The population is all city residents, but the sample is taken only at a bus stop.
This is location bias: the spot chosen guarantees an unrepresentative subgroup, namely bus riders.
People who drive, bike, or walk have little or no chance of being surveyed, so the sample cannot mirror how all residents commute.

items.prompt: A school of $600$ students wants opinions on a new dress code. Three plans are proposed: (1) survey the basketball team, (2) draw $60$ student ID numbers from a hat and survey those students, (3) ask any student who wishes to email an opinion. Which plan gives the most representative sample, and why?
items.answer: Plan 2. Drawing ID numbers from a hat is random, so every student has an equal chance of being chosen, which tends to produce a representative sample.

steps: Plan 1 surveys only one team, an unrepresentative subgroup, so it is biased.
Plan 3 is a voluntary response sample, so only students who choose to email are heard, which is also biased by self-selection.
Plan 2 draws ID numbers at random, giving every one of the $600$ students an equal chance, so it tends to produce a representative sample. Plan 2 is best.

items.prompt: A survey asks: 'Don't you agree that our wonderful library should stay open later?' Explain why the results of this survey may be biased even if many people answer.
items.answer: The question is a leading question. Its wording pushes people toward agreeing, so the responses reflect the wording rather than people's true opinions, and a large number of answers does not remove this bias.

steps: The phrasing 'Don't you agree' and the word 'wonderful' nudge respondents to say yes.
This is a leading question, a source of bias caused by the wording itself, not by who is asked.
Because the wording skews answers, the results are not trustworthy no matter how many people respond.

items.prompt: Two plans are proposed to sample $40$ students from a school of $800$. Plan A: survey the first $40$ students who arrive at school in the morning. Plan B: number all $800$ students and use a random number generator to pick $40$. Which plan is less biased, and why?
items.answer: Plan B. The random number generator gives every student an equal chance, while Plan A oversamples early arrivers, so Plan B is less biased.

steps: Plan A surveys whoever arrives first, which favors students who come early and is a convenience sample.
Plan B numbers every student and selects with a random number generator, giving each of the $800$ an equal chance.
Equal chance of selection makes Plan B a random sample, so Plan B is less biased than Plan A.

items.prompt: From a random sample of $40$ of the $500$ books in a library, $10$ are mysteries. A student estimates the number of mystery books in the whole library. Find the estimate, and state whether this inference is valid given how the sample was chosen.
items.answer: Estimate: about $125$ mystery books. The inference is valid because the sample was random and therefore representative.

steps: Find the sample proportion of mysteries: $\frac{10}{40} = \frac{1}{4}$.
Scale up to the population of $500$: $\frac{1}{4} \times 500 = 125$.
Because the $40$ books were chosen at random, the sample is representative, so the estimate of about $125$ mystery books is a valid inference.

items.prompt: A store wants to know what fraction of its $2000$ customers would use a new delivery service. A manager surveys $500$ customers, but only those shopping between 9 a.m. and 11 a.m. on a weekday. Of those, $300$ say yes, so the manager concludes that $\frac{300}{500}$, or $60\%$, of all customers would use it. Is this conclusion valid? Explain, and note that the large sample size does not fix the problem.
items.answer: No. The sample is biased because it includes only weekday-morning shoppers, who are not representative of all customers. A large sample does not remove this bias, so the $60\%$ conclusion is not justified.

steps: The proportion $\frac{300}{500} = 60\%$ is computed correctly, but correct arithmetic does not make the inference valid.
The sample was taken only on a weekday morning, so it oversamples one type of shopper and misses evening and weekend customers: this is location and time bias.
Increasing the sample size to $500$ does not fix bias; a large sample can still be unrepresentative.
Because the sample is not representative, the conclusion that $60\%$ of all $2000$ customers would use the service is not justified.

items.prompt: In a random sample of $60$ of the $1500$ students in a district, $24$ say they walk to school. Estimate how many of the $1500$ students walk to school, and explain why this estimate can be trusted.
items.answer: About $600$ students. The estimate can be trusted because the sample was random, so it is representative of the district.

steps: Sample proportion who walk: $\frac{24}{60} = \frac{2}{5}$.
Scale up to the population: $\frac{2}{5} \times 1500 = 600$.
Since the $60$ students were selected at random, every student had an equal chance, making the sample representative.
Therefore the estimate of about $600$ walkers is trustworthy.

items.prompt: A club president posts an online poll on the club's fan page asking, 'Should we host the year-end party at the beach?' Of $200$ responses, $180$ say yes, so the president reports that $90\%$ of all club members want the beach. Identify two reasons this inference about all members may be invalid.
items.answer: Reason 1: It is a voluntary response sample, so only members who chose to answer and who visit the fan page are counted (self-selection bias). Reason 2: Members without internet access or who do not follow the page had no chance to respond, so the sample is not representative of all members, and the $90\%$ figure cannot be generalized.

steps: First, the poll is a voluntary response sample: members opt in, so those with strong opinions or who frequent the page are overrepresented.
Second, members who are not on the fan page or lack internet access cannot respond, so part of the population is excluded.
Both issues mean the sample is not representative, so even though $\frac{180}{200} = 90\%$ is computed correctly, the inference about all members is invalid.

items.prompt: A researcher wants to estimate the average number of hours all $3000$ students in a college sleep. Plan X surveys $1000$ students leaving an all-night study room during finals week. Plan Y randomly selects $100$ students from the full enrollment list. Explain which plan gives a more trustworthy estimate, and why a smaller sample can beat a larger one here.
items.answer: Plan Y. Even though it samples only $100$ students, the random selection makes it representative, while Plan X's $1000$ students are biased toward people awake studying during finals, so size does not overcome the bias. Plan Y gives the more trustworthy estimate.

steps: Plan X surveys students leaving an all-night study room during finals, a group very likely to sleep less than average: this is a biased, unrepresentative subgroup.
Plan Y randomly selects from the full enrollment list, so every student has an equal chance and the sample mirrors the population.
A representative sample of $100$ supports a valid inference, while a biased sample of $1000$ does not; sample size alone cannot fix bias.
Therefore Plan Y, despite being smaller, gives the more trustworthy estimate of average sleep.
